title: Are you guys even making money or simply burning cash ?
author: AcanthisittaAware870
selftext: Hey people, I see a lot of you are creating games but are you guys really making money on Steam? I see a lot of games are going into the abyss and I see people burning thousands of dollars, paying Steam fees, and making nothing at all. Is it even the right approach?

comments.author: Aeweisafemalesheep
comments.body: Gabe needs another submarine. Please post your "game."

comments.author: Torschlusspaniker

comments.author: Putrid_Clue_2127
comments.body:
There's been success stories on here. What it comes down to is I feel like a majority of people have this idea in their head of what they want thejr game to be, and then they work on it a little bit, but they never actually polish it up and do the required testing. Just because we're using AI doesn't mean you don't need to be doing a LOT of iterations and test playthroughs. You also have to be able to take a step back from your llm and look at things objectively and know when to give it the right directions with things. Otherwise it can just keep churning out slop. So many people just accept the first couple iterations of whatever their llm comes up with and think they have original assets with gameplay. It just doesn't really work like that. Infact if you're relying solely on your llm to churn out assets from basic prompts, it's going to end up taking a lot of liberties with ideas that already exist and throw them into your own assets. You have to be able to give it actual direction on what to create. 

I think a lot of people believe that it's going to be so much simpler than it is when they go into it. And they either give up before the end product, or they ship out something thats so unpolished nobody will buy it. I also think a lot of people believe they have an original idea that turns out to be not so original and they aren't able to put their own twist on it in a way that appeals to others.

replies.author: karlpilkington4
replies.body: Yup exactly this. Its a lot of testing, fixing bugs, taking a step back and realizing a part of a level isnt even fun, etc.

replies.author: BHTAelitepwn
replies.body: Luckily, AI is really good at fixing bugs. But not good enough at spotting them

replies.author: Squishy_Red_Potato
replies.body: The last 20% of a game takes about 80% of the total time.

comments.author: ichivictus
comments.body: Well before ai, people burned cash in the form of commissioning artists and spending 1+ years of their life and end up not breaking even. AI just makes it a quicker process to realize none of this is financially worth it. Do it for the passion. If it takes off, great. If not, at least you can say you made something.

replies.author: scylk2
replies.body:
Full vibe coding doesn't really make sense if you do it for the passion tho.  
However if you use AI as a teaching assistant, it's amazing. It can help you avoid many pitfalls and steer you in the right direction, while still letting you figure things out and learn. 100% recommend, and it's also probably a lot cheaper.

replies.author: ichivictus
replies.body: I'm not going to gatekeep what anyone thinks is a passion project. If you really enjoy doing something and you spend a ton of time and effort completing a project, that's good enough for me.

replies.author: caesium23
replies.body: Completely depends what your passion is.

replies.author: Bonelessgummybear
replies.body: I feel like vibe coding has changed or how we build changed from it. Vibe coding is the lazy way, I think the new phrase is agentic engineering or something similar. You don't get a fun game without putting in all the other work in.

replies.author: Outrageous-Song5799
replies.body: You can be a game creator and not know how to code the same way a movie realisator doesn’t know how to operate a camera. Stop with the gate keeping

replies.author: PwnCall
replies.body: Ai make you poor faster. Understood

comments.author: Arkenhammer
comments.body: Only about 1000 new games on Steam make any real money each year. Before the AI boom that was about 5% of 20000 new releases. The AI wave has significantly increased the number of new games  but has had essentially no impact on the pool of games that are actually making money.

comments.author: False-Car-1218
comments.body:
Trying to make profit from your game is like winning the lottery, you'll end up burning thousands of dollars and get burnt out

Even seasoned game devs that have been making games for over a decade will tell you that but now with AI it's even worse due to competition

replies.author: AcanthisittaAware870
replies.body: I see that with people, I think people should take their time to polish instead of throwing it to steam fingers crossed.

replies.author: False-Car-1218
replies.body: Marketing, advertising, etc. Matters a lot more than polishing a game, megabonk for example was buggy at the start yet sold millions as well as that chameleon game, you just need to get lucky and hope that it goes viral which is a 0.0001% chance so if you're in game dev to make money then you should do something else

replies.author: Brettinabox
replies.body: As a kid I was told luck wasn't exactly luck, but more about putting yourself in the best position for good things to happen. It still takes a lot of work and you dont know how it will pay off but if the work doesnt happen, it 100% won't.

replies.author: Neither_Berry_100
replies.body:
This. Round up a large collection of games, AI or not. Total revenue. Subtract total costs. Divide by total hours worked. The result will be under minimum wage for sure. Probably much lower.

I've said this many times and will say it again. Making indie games is not a business or job. It is a hobby. You don't make money. At best it is a lottery ticket.

I dont see big companies taking responsibility for all this pile of sht so it is probably going to be us  LOL. Well in a way we are already paying the price of our own actions take a look at hardware prices.

comments.author: Right-Statement367
comments.body: Something tells me that good amount of us here has nothing to do with gamedev and we are all learning here. Personally for me ai is definitely a tool and every project I learn something new. Sometimes for me the goal is not even finishing the game, but to learn a decent pipeline that could help me to build my dream game that is on pause right now :))

comments.author: Reditoxaz
comments.body:
Reality is this: everyone can make extremely good looking PoC/Demo that might even land you 1k+ upvotes in week. Making anything with AI is stupidly easy, but the last 20% of the game/app you make will take u months because AI doesn't see the edge cases, design flaws.



In the end even if you do finish your game its based on luck if it gets at least modestly viral

comments.author: CrimsonBolt33
comments.body: good games still take time...I plan to make at least some money, hopefully....but I am currently just paying a few subscriptions and working my day job...nothing too crazy.

comments.author: Fancy-Proof-9449
comments.body:
Honest answer from me: no. Not Steam, mine is a free Android game that launched last week. Under a hundred installs so far and zero sales. Turned out most people who tapped buy were getting an error, which I only found in my own stats, so that's what I'm fixing first, not the marketing.

What I'd add to the thread: the cash burn is the part you control. No paid ads, no commissioned art, every visual drawn in code and every sound synthesized. Keeping costs that low is what lets me keep going while it's small.

comments.author: mrdzyn
comments.body: Lots enjoying their own creations!

comments.author: Dasshteek
comments.body: I am having fun!

comments.author: PrimeMammothDev
comments.body: I'm making them for fun, if people like it great. Running this as a business is a risky bet, takes a lot of time, effort and care to release a good game, can't just throw money at it

comments.author: Snownova
comments.body:
I'm burning cash, but I'm doing it as a hobby and passion project. I tried making this game 10 years ago but stopped due to time constraints and my artwork being unworthy of the concept.

Now I finally get to make my dream come true and play that updated version of one of my childhood's favourite games.

I wrote a book that sold like 50 copies too. I don't care, I enjoyed writing it and that's all that matters to me.

comments.author: richchiudev
comments.body:
>Realistically, 90% of us are definitely burning time and money rather than making a living off this. Steam is insanely crowded, and simply uploading a finished game and praying for sales almost guarantees it disappears into the abyss.  
For my current project, I'm treating it as a passion project with strict budget limits—no dropping thousands of dollars I can't afford to lose. Instead, I'm trying to focus on building a small community and testing with real players *early* before even thinking about launch. If you treat it like an expensive hobby that *might* pay off someday, it hurts a lot less than betting your savings on it!

comments.author: Tri8ar
comments.body:
Well, it's a hobby side project for me, so I don't put in any money I'd be afraid to lose.

It's fun in its own way: I learn a ton, think a ton, and it costs a fraction of what classic hobbies like fishing or tabletop gaming do. And the experience is tailor-made like nothing before. I can explore any theme to whatever depth I want, without waiting for someone else to make it for me.

I have a high bar for quality, so I iterate the hell out of everything. Maybe it's all for nothing, but that's just how I'm wired, and maybe it'll be worth someone's while. If not, well, at least I've built something instead of burning my time on time sinks and social media.

So no, I'm not aiming to get rich from my creations, but a small community around them would be nice.

comments.author: TemporaryQuiet1337
comments.body: I build games for myself tbh and I don't care about making money off of them

comments.author: BlendedSmarts
comments.body:
First off, just because you play games doesn't mean you can make games. People are making games with AI that have no business making a game. AI has removed the barrier for entry, which is fine as long as you know what the hell you are doing. 99% of people have no clue how to make a game and it shows.

Secondly, even if you know how to make a game, AI isn't going to solve how you bring a game to market and essentially sell a game. 99% of the developers, even those not using AI to make their game, have no clue how to market their game. Even with AI giving them recommendations, they have no clue what market they made their game for and just think pushing it on Steam, making a few YouTube videos etc is good enough.

Lastly, you are making a product at the end of the day. People are going to burn cash trying to push that product having **ZERO EXPERIENCE** doing this in the past. So naturally, lots of people are failing to launch.

comments.author: Victorbar974
comments.body: I approach this from another angle , it is true that not everyone are skilled game devs , myself included , however the massive flax of games allows to choose the very best and it is like a rapid evolution compared to the pressed AI times, I think that everyone should follow his passion and allow thr game evolution to decide if the game is indeed worthy or not and if not , just try again . One thing I think is obvious right now is that the game categorization needs to evolve too , we simply don't have the time to try out all games , so we need to choose by thr exact game category we love and perhaps develop completely new categories , like educational tycoon category, or non fictional incremental strategy etc...

comments.author: Post-reality
comments.body: I'm almost 2 months in since the beginning of the development, and I'm no where near release whatsoever. Call me 2-3 years from now lol, or earlier if I'm lucky. That being said, I saw a few releases from here and they went successful from financial perspective, so if you put effort (and have ab original idea) I believe that it's doable to have a success.

comments.author: StellarSoupStudio
comments.body: Nope this is a hobby for me, one I'm putting a bit of effort into because hey why not, but one I do not expect will make money. It has taught me how to use coding agents in a better way, taught me how to log user telemetry, and set up better CI/CD systems. I'm also only on the $20 dollar a month claude subscription and I only release to my personal website and itch.

comments.author: deege
comments.body: This isn’t true. For years the common advice was to make small games so you didn’t spend years on a game. The idea was to get 3-4 games out a year if you were looking to be in the business of making indie games. That was the strategy long before AI.

replies.author: Good-Acanthaceae-136
replies.body:
It's not really about making money, that can be true if you're already a small game dev studio but it's not generally the mentality of a solo developer.

The idea of making simple games is more to do with scope. Simple games force you to keep your scope within reach so you have more chance of actually finishing a game.  When you let your scope creep you end up with Star Citizen.

Unfortunately AI has kind of destroyed the idea of simple games now unless you are a really good artist. They will just be instantly copied if they get even the slightest amount of traction.
